claims.text: Introducing a thin Ni transition interlayer will enhance interface coherency in HEA multilayers.
Enhanced interface coherency produced by a Ni interlayer will mediate conversion between diffusion-mediated and dislocation-mediated creep.
The initial HEA multilayers have coherent interfaces.
The initial HEA multilayers lack a specialized interlayer for modulating creep mechanisms.
A controlled thin Ni layer is to be deposited between HEA layers.
Creep is prominent under the proposed high-temperature conditions.
Irradiation and corrosive environments are typical operating conditions for these advanced coatings.
A Ni interlayer can remain coherent with HEA layers.
Ni provides lattice matching with HEAs such as CoCrFeMnNi.
Ni has moderate diffusivity under the relevant creep conditions.
The FCC structure of Ni supports dislocation glide.
The Ni layer will reduce atomic migration at lower temperatures.
Reduced atomic migration at lower temperatures will favor dislocation-mediated creep.
The Ni layer will permit diffusion-mediated creep at higher temperatures.
Adding the Ni interlayer will cause a measurable shift in creep rate and dominant creep mechanism relative to samples without Ni.
HEA multilayers without Ni are dominated solely by either diffusion-mediated or dislocation-mediated creep and lack controlled modulation between them.
The predicted effect is limited to temperature and stress regimes in which diffusion and dislocation activity are both operative.
Extremely high temperatures may eliminate interface coherency and suppress the proposed effect.
The creep-rate shift and transition thresholds depend on Ni-interlayer thickness, HEA composition, and operating conditions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism assigns dislocation-mediated creep to lower temperatures and diffusion-mediated creep to higher temperatures, whereas the predicted outcome describes the transition direction as diffusion-dominated to dislocation-dominated without specifying a different control axis.
